readerTitle: They explained the change clearly. Output still collapsed.
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Coch & French, 1948, Harwood 의류 공장) + 가상 적용 (공장 판단 문제, 소프트웨어 회사 판단 문제)
insight: 변화를 이끌 때 리더는 '무엇을'과 '왜'를 정하고, '어떻게'는 그 일을 하는 사람들과 함께 정한다. 저항은 변화 자체보다 통제와 능력을 잃는 데서 생긴다.
misconception: 변화에 대한 저항은 더 좋은 설명이나 압박으로 이겨낼 수 있다. 사람들은 원래 변화를 싫어한다.

sources.text: Coch, L., & French, J. R. P. (1948). Overcoming Resistance to Change. Human Relations, 1(4), 512–532.
French, J. R. P., Israel, J., & Ås, D. (1960). An Experiment on Participation in a Norwegian Factory. Human Relations, 13(1), 3–19.
판단 문제의 공장과 소프트웨어 회사는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Coch & French 실험의 대조군(참여 없음) 설명: 회의에서 경쟁 상황 때문에 변화가 필요하다는 설명을 들었다는 점을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요.
대조군이 약 40일 안에 약 17%(카드에는 'about one in six') 퇴사했고 생산량이 회복되지 않았다는 수치를 원문으로 확인하세요. 전원 참여 집단이 며칠 안에 회복하고 이전 생산량을 넘었다는 내용도 확인이 필요합니다.
대조군 잔류 인원을 몇 주 뒤 다시 모아 전원 참여 방식으로 새 작업에 배치했더니 빠르게 회복했다는 후속 결과가 원문에 있는지 확인하세요.
노르웨이 공장 재현 연구(French, Israel & Ås, 1960)의 효과가 더 약했고, 참여가 정당하고 중요한 사안으로 인식될 때만 효과가 컸다는 요약이 맞는지 확인하세요. 카드에는 일반적인 표현으로만 적었습니다.

cards.title: They explained the change clearly. Output still collapsed.
body: In the 1940s, a pajama factory in Virginia kept hitting the same wall. Each time it changed how a job was done, output fell, tempers rose and people quit.
The changes were small. Managers explained them. It didn't help. So two researchers ran an experiment to find out why.

image.label: Sewing workers at machines, one empty chair
image.brief: 1940년대 느낌의 의류 공장. 재봉틀 앞에 작업자들이 앉아 있고 한 자리만 비어 있음. 벽에는 'New method' 공지문. 따뜻하지만 약간 긴장된 분위기. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You must change how a job is done.
body: You run a packing line at a factory. A big customer now wants smaller boxes, so the line's steps must change. The deadline and cost target are fixed.
How do you bring the team through it?

options.text: Hold a meeting, explain why the change is needed, then roll out the new method
options.feedback: Fast and clear. But people hear a decision about their work made without them, and their know-how gets ignored.

options.text: Ask two team representatives to help design the new method
options.feedback: Better than a top-down rollout, and quicker than involving everyone. The rest of the team still receives a plan instead of shaping it.

options.text: Share the fixed target, then have the whole team design the new steps with you
options.feedback: It costs a few hours up front. In return, the people who do the work spot problems early and own the result.

cards.title: The explained group fell apart.
body: At the Harwood factory, researchers Lester Coch and John French tested the three approaches you just saw.
One group was told in a meeting that competition made the change necessary. Others helped design the new methods, through representatives or all together.

The told group's output dropped and stayed low. Hostility toward managers grew, and within about 40 days roughly one in six had quit. The groups where everyone took part recovered quickly, then beat their old output.

cards.title: Leading change: share the how
body: **Leading change** means deciding *what* must change and *why*, then letting the people who do the work help decide *how*.
People rarely resist change itself. They resist losing control, losing skills they were proud of, and being treated as if their experience doesn't count. Participation gives those things back.

image.label: Three zones: What, Why, How
image.brief: 세 개의 원이 이어진 인포그래픽. 'What'과 'Why' 원 옆에는 리더 아이콘, 'How' 원 안에는 여러 팀원 아이콘이 모여 함께 손을 얹고 있음. 깔끔한 플랫 스타일.

cards.title: Same people, different result.
body: The most telling part came later. Weeks after the first test, the researchers reportedly gathered what remained of the told group and moved them to a new job, this time with full participation.
They recovered quickly, like the other groups had. The problem was never the workers. It was how the change reached them.
cards.callout: Resistance is often a signal about the process, not about the people.

cards.title: Be clear about what is open.
body: Participation doesn't mean everything is up for a vote. Good change leaders split the decision in three:
Say each part out loud. People can accept a firm deadline if they really own the steps.
list: **Fixed:** the goal, the deadline, the budget
**Open for input:** options you'll weigh before deciding
**Yours to decide:** the how, within those limits
cards.softwareNote: The same split works when moving a team to a new tool or process: the date and the goal are fixed, and the team designs the setup, the pilot and the rules.

cards.title: Fake participation is worse than none.
body: Asking for input on a decision already made teaches people that their voice is for show. Later studies, including one in a Norwegian factory, found weaker effects when workers didn't see the participation as real or the issue as important.
Participation also takes time. In a true emergency, you may have to decide first and explain after.

cards.title: Now it's a software team.
body: You lead 30 engineers at a software company. The CEO has decided the team will move from monthly releases to weekly ones by the end of next quarter. Some engineers are already grumbling.

options.text: Present a strong case for weekly releases, set the date and book training
options.feedback: Clear and well argued, much like the told group at Harwood. You'll get compliance, but the people who know where releases break aren't shaping the plan.

options.text: Share why and the fixed deadline, then have the team design the process and run a pilot
options.feedback: The goal stays firm while engineers own the how. Their objections become design input instead of quiet resistance.

options.text: Ask the team whether they want to move to weekly releases at all
options.feedback: It feels respectful, but the decision is already made. If you then overrule them, you've staged fake participation and lost trust.

cards.title: Decide the what and why. Share the how.
body: A clear explanation isn't enough. People commit to change they helped shape.
**Try it today:** pick one change you're planning. Write down what is fixed, what is open for input, and what the team can decide. Then tell them all three.
